title: OGAM: Connecting Systematic Testing to Runtime Assurance through Object-Grounded Attention Monitoring for VLA Policies
action_head: mixed: discrete action tokens (OpenVLA), regression head with 8-step chunks (OpenVLA-OFT), UniVLA (head not described in text read), flow/diffusion action expert (pi0.5, 50-step chunks, 10 executed)
methods: pairwise combinatorial instruction generation from scene objects and action templates, LLM feasibility labels with blind human review
gradient-weighted visual attention per action query, projected onto object masks
instruction-role channels (named targets, strongest competitor, remainder, gripper)
open-end DTW against one successful reference per task (on-track and completion readouts)
success-only leave-one-out conformal calibration of a sustained-deviation stop rule (nominal alpha = 0.05)
question: Can systematic instruction testing expose VLA failures beyond benchmarks, and can object-grounded attention trajectories compared to successful references stop failing episodes early without failure labels?
key_findings: None of the four policies completes any of the 24 feasible pairwise-generated instructions in the LIBERO-Goal task-0 scene (87 generated instructions: 24 feasible, 62 infeasible, 1 hazardous; LLM-human agreement 85%).
Behavior substitution: OpenVLA executed or visibly attempted a trained task in 43 of 87 episodes, and 13 episodes produced unrequested hazards (bottle tipping, bowl dropped, stove left on).
Paraphrases alone (130 per policy, same scene and goal) cut success to 48% (OpenVLA), 81% (UniVLA), 88% (OFT), 92% (pi0.5), versus 10/10 on canonical instructions.

OGAM stops 87-100% of failed paraphrase episodes with 3-5% observed false stops, median stop at 5-12 s of a 20 s budget, saving 39-72% of failing-episode time; calibrated thresholds q = 1.99, 1.79, 2.83, 2.04 for OpenVLA, OFT, UniVLA, pi0.5.

Ablations: each readout alone loses up to 24 points of detection; simpler signals under the same rule do worse (role-vector distance about 44%, target attention share about 40%, per the partly garbled ablation text); replacing simulator masks with Grounding DINO + SAM 2 costs 5 points on OpenVLA with no extra false stops.
In generated-instruction episodes, early attention share on an unnamed but engaged object is 0.26 vs 0.06 for non-engaging episodes (AUC 0.79).

benchmarks: LIBERO-Goal (10 tasks, fixed initial states, deterministic execution)
LIBERO-Para paraphrase types (130 instructions per policy)
evidence.scale: one deterministic rollout per instruction; failures available for detection: about 67 (OpenVLA), 25 (UniVLA), 15 (OFT), 11 (pi0.5) paraphrase failures out of 130
evidence.statistics: partial: conformal calibration with a nominal 5% target (authors state no finite-sample guarantee for their jackknife variant); no CIs on detection rates
evidence.baselines: single-readout variants, role-vector distance to successes, target attention share, action-chunk consistency (named in ablation text)

causal_validation: No. Attention is used purely as a monitored signal; the paper explicitly sidesteps whether attention explains behavior and validates only its usefulness for early stopping.
closed_loop: Monitoring is evaluated on closed-loop rollouts, but stop times are reconstructed offline from recorded episodes rather than by stopping the robot online.
limitations_stated: Split-conformal finite-sample guarantee does not strictly apply to the jackknife reuse of successes; observed false-stop rates are empirical.
Object poses held fixed to isolate linguistic variation; pose factors left as an extension.
critique: Detection rates for the stronger policies rest on very few failures (about 11-15 for pi0.5 and OFT), so 87-100% has wide uncertainty that is not reported.
Deterministic simulation with fixed initial states and one reference per task makes DTW-to-reference unusually clean; robustness to scene and pose variation is untested.

The 'no feasible generated instruction succeeds' result is striking but comes from one scene and one rollout per instruction; it is behavioral evidence that LIBERO-trained VLAs map scenes to trained trajectories regardless of the request, consistent with 2603.06001 and 2604.18000.

Gradient-weighted attention is a mix of attention and gradient, so the monitor is not evidence about attention heads per se; still, the role-channel design makes it comparable across four architectures, which is rare in this literature.
one_line: Combinatorial instruction tests show four LIBERO-trained VLAs fail every new feasible request and often substitute trained behaviors, and a monitor that compares object-grounded attention courses to successful references via DTW stops most failing episodes early with few false stops.
